definition:
In the Bible a name is more than a label. It says who someone is, carries their reputation, and gives others a way to call on them. So when God reveals his names he is making himself known and making himself available: his people can call on his name, swear by it, bless in it, and be called by it. The Hebrew word is shem, ‘name’, which can also mean reputation or renown, and the Greek is onoma. To speak of God's ‘name’ is often to speak of God himself as he has made himself known, which is why the Psalms can say, “O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is Your name in all the earth” (Psalm 8:1), and why the third commandment forbids taking the name of the LORD “in vain” (Exodus 20:7), that is, using it for nothing, falsely, or to no good end. This study traces the names and titles by which God makes himself known; the study of who God is treats the basic confession of one God, and the study of the Trinity treats the triune name.

The main Old Testament names are these. 'Elohim, the ordinary word for God, is plural in form but takes singular verbs when it refers to Israel's God; it occurs about 2,600 times. 'El, the older and shorter word for a god, appears alone and in titles such as 'El 'Elyon, ‘God Most High’, 'El Shaddai, ‘God Almighty’, 'El Ro'i, ‘the God who sees’, and 'El 'Olam, ‘the Eternal God’. 'Adonai, ‘Lord’ or ‘my Lord’, is a title of mastery. Above all stands YHWH, God's personal name, which appears nearly 6,800 times. Most English Bibles, including the BSB, print it as LORD in small capital letters and print 'Adonai as Lord; where the two stand together they print ‘Lord GOD’. The Greek Old Testament rendered YHWH as kyrios, ‘Lord’, and the New Testament follows it, while adding the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and giving Jesus the title Lord.
ot:
Genesis introduces God first as 'Elohim, the Creator (Genesis 1:1), and from the second chapter as “the LORD God” (Genesis 2:4 onward), joining the Creator of all to Israel's covenant God. The patriarchs meet God under several titles, often tied to a place or an event. Melchizedek blesses Abram by “God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth,” and Abram answers by naming “the LORD God Most High” (Genesis 14:19-22), identifying the high God with the LORD. Hagar names the one who spoke to her “the God who sees me” (Genesis 16:13). God appears to Abram as “God Almighty” (Genesis 17:1), the Hebrew 'El Shaddai; Shaddai, alone or with 'El, occurs about forty-eight times, most of them in Job. Its origin is uncertain: proposals connect it with a word for mountain, with a word for breast, or, in an old Jewish explanation, with ‘the one who is sufficient’; the Greek translators often rendered it pantokratōr and the Latin omnipotens, which gave English ‘Almighty’. Abraham calls on “the LORD, the Eternal God” at Beersheba (Genesis 21:33), and Jacob names an altar El-Elohe-Israel, ‘God, the God of Israel’ (Genesis 33:20). Texts excavated at Ugarit in Syria from 1929 onward show that El was also the name of the chief god of the Canaanite pantheon; Israel used the common word for God but filled it with its own confession.

The decisive moment comes at the burning bush. Moses asks what name to give the Israelites, and God answers, “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14), then names himself the LORD, “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” adding, “This is My name forever” (Exodus 3:15). The text links the name YHWH to the Hebrew verb hayah, ‘to be’ or ‘to become’, and God's answer, 'ehyeh 'asher 'ehyeh, uses the same form he has just used in promising Moses, “I will surely be with you” (Exodus 3:12). The name therefore speaks both of God's self-existence and of his faithful presence, and interpreters weigh the two differently. Exodus 6:2-3 then says that God appeared to the patriarchs as God Almighty but did not make himself known to them by his name the LORD, though Genesis has the patriarchs using the name, and since Genesis 4:26 people had called on it; the ways of reading this are set out below. Most importantly, at Sinai the LORD proclaims his name and then describes it: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:5-7). God's name is filled with his character.

The personal name was eventually not spoken aloud in Jewish practice, out of reverence and in view of Exodus 20:7 and Leviticus 24:16. When the Masoretes, the scribes who added vowel signs to the Hebrew text in the early Middle Ages, came to YHWH, they wrote the vowels of 'Adonai (or sometimes 'Elohim) with it to tell the reader what to say aloud. The pronunciation ‘Yahweh’ is a scholarly reconstruction, supported by the short form Yah (as in ‘Hallelujah’, ‘praise Yah’) and by early Greek transcriptions. The form ‘Jehovah’ arose from reading the consonants of the name with the vowels of 'Adonai; it entered English in William Tyndale's translation of the Pentateuch (1530) and appears a few times in the King James Version.

The rest of the Old Testament adds titles that each disclose part of who God is. 'Adonai emphasizes his lordship. “The LORD of Hosts,” YHWH Tseva'ot, first appears in 1 Samuel 1:3 and is used more than two hundred times, above all in the prophets; the ‘hosts’ are the armies of heaven and earth under his command. Isaiah's favorite title, “the Holy One of Israel,” which he uses about twenty-five times, joins God's otherness to his bond with his people (Isaiah 41:14). God is the Rock (Deuteronomy 32:4), Shepherd (Psalm 23:1), King, Redeemer (Isaiah 44:6), and, more rarely, Father (Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16; 64:8; Malachi 1:6). Daniel sees the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:9). Several popular ‘compound names’ are really names given to places or altars in response to what God did: The LORD Will Provide (Genesis 22:14), The LORD Is My Banner (Exodus 17:15), The LORD Is Peace (Judges 6:24), and THE LORD IS THERE, the name of the restored city (Ezekiel 48:35). Jeremiah gives the coming king the name “The LORD Our Righteousness” (Jeremiah 23:6). These are true confessions about God, but they are not a list of separate divine names to be invoked one by one.

The Old Testament also develops a theology of the name itself. God chooses a place “as a dwelling for His Name” (Deuteronomy 12:5), and Solomon prays toward the temple where God said, “My Name shall be there” (1 Kings 8:29): God is present by his name without being contained. He leads “for the sake of His name” (Psalm 23:3), and he acts to save Israel not for their sake “but for My holy name, which you profaned among the nations” (Ezekiel 36:22). “The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run to it and are safe” (Proverbs 18:10). The prophets look ahead to a day when “My name will be great among the nations” (Malachi 1:11) and “the LORD alone, and His name alone” will be confessed over all the earth (Zechariah 14:9).
nt:
The New Testament begins by naming a child. Joseph is told to call him Jesus “because He will save His people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Jesus is the Greek form of the Hebrew Yeshua, a later form of Joshua, whose name means ‘the LORD saves’; the explanation in Matthew depends on that meaning. Matthew adds the name from Isaiah 7:14, Immanuel, “which means, ‘God with us’” (Matthew 1:23). Jesus taught his disciples to pray, “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name” (Matthew 6:9): the first petition asks God to make his own name honored as holy, the fulfillment of what Ezekiel promised. In John's Gospel Jesus sums up his work as revealing that name: “I have revealed Your name to those You have given Me” (John 17:6), and he asks the “Holy Father” to protect them by “the name You gave Me” (John 17:11).

Father becomes the characteristic Christian name for God, and it has a particular shape. Jesus prayed “Abba, Father” in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), and Paul says the Spirit enables believers to cry the same words (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). Abba is Aramaic, the word a child or adult used for a father. Joachim Jeremias argued in the twentieth century that Jesus' use of it in prayer was without close parallel, and popular preaching took this to mean ‘Daddy’. James Barr showed in 1988 that the word was also used by adults and does not carry the childish sense; the intimacy of the word lies in Jesus' relationship as the Son, into which believers are adopted, not in a nursery term. Matthew 28:19 then gathers the names into one: disciples are baptized “in the name,” singular, “of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

The New Testament also gives Jesus the name that belonged to Israel's God. Because the Greek Old Testament rendered YHWH as kyrios, the earliest Christian confession, “Jesus is Lord” (Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3), carried the sound of the divine name. Paul immediately supports it by quoting Joel 2:32, “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13), where the Lord in Joel is YHWH and the Lord in Romans is Jesus. The Aramaic prayer marana tha, preserved in 1 Corinthians 16:22 (“Come, O Lord”), shows Aramaic-speaking believers calling on Jesus as Lord very early. God has given Jesus “the name above all names” so that every knee bows at the name of Jesus (Philippians 2:9-10); interpreters debate whether the name given is ‘Lord’ itself or the name Jesus now filled with divine honor, but either way the passage applies Isaiah 45:23, where the one God swears every knee will bow to him. In Acts the apostles heal, preach, and baptize in Jesus' name, and Peter says, “there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

John's Gospel adds Jesus' absolute ‘I am’ sayings, the Greek egō eimi used without a predicate. Jesus says, “unless you believe that I am He, you will die in your sins” (John 8:24), and “before Abraham was born, I am” (John 8:58). The Greek Old Testament used egō eimi in Isaiah's declarations that the LORD alone is God (Isaiah 43:10) and in Exodus 3:14, and when Jesus says “I am He” in the garden, those who came to arrest him fall to the ground (John 18:5-6). Revelation brings the names to their end. God is “Him who is and was and is to come” (Revelation 1:4), a title many interpreters read as an expansion of Exodus 3:14; John keeps it in the nominative case even after a preposition that requires another case, as if the name could not be declined. God is “the Alpha and the Omega” (Revelation 1:8), and Jesus claims the same title (Revelation 22:13). The conqueror receives “a new name” (Revelation 2:17), Christ bears a name “that only He Himself knows” and is called “The Word of God” and “KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS” (Revelation 19:12-16), and in the new creation God's servants “will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads” (Revelation 22:4).

keyTexts.why: Melchizedek blesses by God Most High, and Abram identifies God Most High with the LORD. The high God and Israel's covenant God are one.
God reveals himself to Abram as God Almighty, El Shaddai, and calls him to walk before him. The chief patriarchal name.
God gives Moses his name: I AM WHO I AM, the LORD, the God of the fathers. The center of the Bible's teaching on God's name.
God says he was known to the patriarchs as God Almighty but not by his name the LORD. A verse read in several ways, all of which stress what the name now means.
The third commandment forbids taking the LORD's name in vain. The name is holy because God has given himself in it.
The LORD proclaims his name and fills it with his character: compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness.
God chooses a place as a dwelling for his Name. He is present to his people by his name without being contained.
I am the LORD; that is my name, and I will not yield my glory to another. The name belongs to the one God alone.
God will act for the sake of his holy name, profaned among the nations. The honor of the name drives his saving work.
The child is named Jesus, the LORD saves, because he will save his people, and Immanuel, God with us.
The first petition of the Lord's Prayer asks that the Father's name be hallowed. Prayer begins with God's name.
Before Abraham was born, I am. Jesus' absolute I am echoes the Greek of Exodus 3:14 and Isaiah.
Confessing Jesus as Lord, Paul applies Joel's promise about calling on the name of the LORD to Jesus.
God gives Jesus the name above every name, and every knee bows to him, as Isaiah said every knee would bow to the LORD.
The Lord God is the Alpha and the Omega, who is and was and is to come. The Bible's last book gathers the names of God into worship.

history:
Reverence for the name shaped Jewish practice before the church began. By the later Second Temple period the personal name was generally not spoken aloud. Some of the Dead Sea Scrolls write it in the older paleo-Hebrew script while the rest of the text is in the square script, and some early Greek copies of the Old Testament, such as Papyrus Fouad 266 (first century BC), keep it in Hebrew letters within the Greek. The Mishnah, compiled around 200, records that the high priest spoke the name on the Day of Atonement and warns against pronouncing it by its letters. Later Jewish usage speaks of HaShem, ‘the Name’. The New Testament writers, writing in Greek, followed the Greek Bible in saying kyrios, and the church inherited the practice.

The church fathers treated the names of God as a school of both knowledge and reverence. Jerome, in a letter to Marcella around 384, listed ten Hebrew names of God. The writer known as Pseudo-Dionysius, around 500, wrote The Divine Names, arguing that God is rightly praised by the names Scripture gives him (good, being, life, wisdom) and yet surpasses every name. The Jewish philosopher Moses Maimonides, in The Guide for the Perplexed (around 1190), held that the four-letter name is the only name of God not drawn from his actions. Thomas Aquinas devoted a question of the Summa Theologiae to the names of God, argued that names apply to God by analogy, and judged ‘He who is’, from Exodus 3:14, the most fitting name of all because it signifies being itself. Reformation Bibles brought the question into English print: Tyndale used ‘Jehovah’ in a few places, and the King James Version (1611) printed LORD for the name in most places and JEHOVAH in a handful.

Modern scholarship added historical questions. In 1753 Jean Astruc suggested that Moses used different sources in Genesis, marked by the names Elohim and YHWH, and the divine names became one starting point for the documentary hypothesis, given its classic form by Julius Wellhausen (1878). The excavation of the Ugaritic texts from 1929 opened comparison with Canaanite religion. At the same time, the name became a mark of identity in new movements: the Jehovah's Witnesses took that name in 1931, and the Sacred Name movement, which arose in the 1930s, taught that the Hebrew names must be pronounced correctly. Translations divided over the name: the Jerusalem Bible (1966) printed ‘Yahweh’ throughout, while most English Bibles kept LORD. In 2008 the Vatican's Congregation for Divine Worship directed that the name not be pronounced in Catholic liturgy, out of respect for Jewish practice and the church's own tradition. In the late twentieth century some theologians, such as Sallie McFague (Models of God, 1987) and Elizabeth Johnson (She Who Is, 1992), argued for feminine names alongside the traditional ones, and others answered that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are revealed names rather than human metaphors. The site has no separate systematic page on this doctrine; the treatment of God and the Trinity at /theology/doctrine/god-and-trinity covers the related questions.

differ.body: Exodus 3:14 discloses that God simply is: he exists from himself, depends on nothing, and cannot be defined by anything outside himself. The Greek translation, ‘I am the one who is’, and Jesus' absolute ‘I am’ sayings point the same way. Defenders in the classical tradition, from Augustine and Aquinas to many modern Reformed and Catholic theologians, hold that this is not Greek philosophy imposed on the text but what the text itself claims, since God answers a question about his name with a statement about his being. The promise of presence follows from it: only the one who is can be with his people in every place and generation.

differ.view: I AM as God's faithful presence
differ.body: Exodus 3:14 is first a promise, ‘I will be who I will be’, spoken to a frightened man about to face Pharaoh. God has just said, ‘I will be with you’ (Exodus 3:12), with the same verb form, and the story that follows shows who he will be by what he does. Defenders, including many Old Testament scholars and theologians in the Reformed, Lutheran, and Jewish traditions, argue that the Hebrew verb speaks of active, dynamic being rather than abstract existence and that the name's meaning is filled in by the exodus and by Exodus 34. Most grant that God's self-existence is implied; they deny that it is the main point.

differ.view: Exodus 6:3: the name's meaning newly revealed
differ.body: The patriarchs knew and used the name, as Genesis shows, but did not know what it meant in its full character as the name of the God who keeps covenant promises and redeems a people from slavery. In Hebrew idiom ‘to know a name’ can mean to know the reality it stands for. Defenders, including most traditional Jewish and Christian interpreters and many modern literary readers, point out that the verses that follow speak of God remembering his covenant and redeeming Israel, which is what the patriarchs had been promised but had not seen.

The verse means what it most naturally says: in the tradition behind it, the name YHWH was first revealed to Moses, and the patriarchs knew God as El Shaddai. Genesis includes material from other traditions in which the name was used from the beginning (Genesis 4:26). Defenders, including many historical-critical scholars since the nineteenth century, see this as one of the clearest signs that the Pentateuch combines earlier sources. Many who hold this view still read the final text as a unity whose editors intended the reader to hear Exodus 6 as the moment the name's meaning comes to light.

errors:
The church has rejected several misuses of God's names. The oldest is treating the name as a magic word, a formula that gives the speaker power whatever their relationship to God. The sons of Sceva tried to use “the name of the Lord Jesus” as an incantation and were overpowered (Acts 19:13-16), and Jesus warned that some who did mighty works in his name would hear that he never knew them (Matthew 7:22-23). The same error appears when ‘in Jesus' name’ is treated as a guarantee that any request must be granted. A related error is taking the name in vain in the old sense: invoking God to back a false oath, a cruelty, a party, or a nation's cause. The third commandment is about far more than profanity.

Other errors concern the names themselves. Some teach that salvation or true worship depends on pronouncing the Hebrew names correctly, as some Sacred Name groups have; but the New Testament apostles wrote kyrios and theos in Greek and called on God in the languages of the nations, and Pentecost shows God's works declared in many tongues. Others treat the Old Testament titles as a menu of separate powers, calling on one name for provision and another for healing, when each names the one God. Still others build doctrine on invented etymologies, such as popular claims that the letters of the name imitate the sound of breathing, which have no basis in Hebrew. The church's confession is simpler: God has made himself known by name, and his name is known truly through what he has said and done, supremely in Jesus Christ.
life:
Because God has a name, he can be called on. The Bible's first act of worship after the fall is that people “began to call upon the name of the LORD” (Genesis 4:26), and its promise is that “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). Christian prayer is not addressed to an unknown force but to one who has introduced himself, and Jesus taught his disciples to begin prayer by asking that God's name be honored before asking for bread or forgiveness. That order shapes a life: it places God's reputation ahead of one's own, and it makes the way a person speaks and acts a matter of carrying God's name well or badly.

The names also give comfort in particular places. The one who is God Most High is the God who sees a runaway servant in the wilderness; the LORD of Hosts is also the Holy One who dwells among his people; the Father is the one whose name Jesus revealed. Christians are baptized into the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and the Bible ends with that name written on the foreheads of those who see God's face. To bear his name is to belong to him.
questions: God answers Moses' request for his name with “I AM WHO I AM” and then fills the name with his character in Exodus 34. What do those two passages together teach about what it means to know God's name?
The first Christians called Jesus kyrios, the word their Greek Bible used for God's personal name. What does Paul's use of Joel 2:32 in Romans 10:13 show about how they understood him?
The third commandment forbids taking the LORD's name in vain. Beyond careless speech, what are some ways people today might use God's name for their own purposes?
